steps: For every entry with a source_url, fetch the abstract (arXiv) or README (GitHub) and extract the published figure.
If a re-read figure differs from the stored one, keep the old value in a history array, write the new one, and set changed:true for review. Never overwrite silently.
If a source cannot be read, keep the stored value, set stale:true, and leave date_refreshed unchanged so the age stays visible.
Only entries with include_in_public_average:true feed the comparison; adding an entry to the average is a manual, reviewed decision.

entries.notes_on_methodology: Abstract: ChatGPT is likely to generate hallucinated content in specific topics by fabricating unverifiable information, about 19.5% of responses. Human-annotated benchmark of generated and real responses; the rate applies to the chosen topics and the 2023-era model, not to LLMs in general.

entries.reported_as: Best model truthful on 58% of questions; human performance 94%
entries.notes_on_methodology: Adversarial questions built to elicit common human misconceptions. It measures truthfulness, not a hallucination rate, and the models are 2021-era, so it is historical context only and is excluded from the average.

A planning range supplied by the site owner, NOT a single published figure. It is the same order of magnitude as HaluEval's 19.5%, but published rates vary enormously with task and model (from 1.8% in grounded summarisation to 58%–88% on legal case queries). Kept for display continuity; excluded from the average.

Top three models when read: 1.8%, 3.1% and 3.3% (leaderboard last updated 2026-05-11). Measures how often a model adds claims not supported by the document it was asked to summarise, scored by Vectara's HHEM-2.3 model over 7,700+ articles. It is a faithfulness-to-source task, much easier than open-book question answering, so it is the best case and must not be compared with closed-book accuracy.

entries.source_name: Vectara Hallucination Leaderboard, full range across models (HHEM)
entries.notes_on_methodology: Range across all models on the leaderboard when read (1.8% to 24.2%). The maintainers state the approach is far from definitive and measures only factual consistency with the source, not summary quality or other kinds of hallucination.

entries.source_name: Stanford RegLab / HAI, Hallucination-Free? Assessing the Reliability of Leading AI Legal Research Tools (Magesh et al.; 2024)
entries.notes_on_methodology: Abstract: Lexis+ AI and Thomson Reuters' Westlaw AI-Assisted Research and Ask Practical Law AI each hallucinate between 17% and 33% of the time. These are retrieval-augmented commercial legal research tools, evaluated on a preregistered set of legal queries. The published upper figure is 33%, not 34%.

entries.source_name: Stanford RegLab / HAI, Large Legal Fictions: Profiling Legal Hallucinations in Large Language Models (Dahl et al.; 2024)
entries.notes_on_methodology: Abstract: legal hallucinations occur between 58% of the time with ChatGPT 4 and 88% with Llama 2 when asked specific, verifiable questions about random federal court cases. General-purpose models without retrieval, 2023-era. Far harsher than legal AI tools, so it is reported separately and excluded from the primary average.

entries.reported_as: Best model F1 as low as 0.625 at detecting 'hard' medical hallucinations (GPT-4o, Llama-3.1, UltraMedical tested)
entries.notes_on_methodology: A hallucination DETECTION benchmark: it scores how well a model spots planted medical hallucinations, not how often a model produces them. An F1 score is not a hallucination rate, so no rate is recorded.

Reasoning- and memory-based hallucination tests over medical question sets. The abstract reports significant differences between models (GPT-3.5, LlaMa-2 and others) but gives no percentage, so no rate is recorded here; take figures from the paper's tables if you need them.

entries.source_name: We Have a Package for You! Package hallucinations by code-generating LLMs (Spracklen et al.; 2024)
entries.notes_on_methodology: Abstract: the average percentage of hallucinated packages is at least 5.2% for commercial models and 21.7% for open-source models. Measures recommended software packages that do not exist. A code-generation task; not comparable to engineering knowledge questions.

entries.reported_as: GPT-4-Turbo with a retrieval system incorrectly answered or refused 81% of questions
entries.notes_on_methodology: 150-case sample of 10,000+ questions on public companies' filings. The 81% counts wrong answers AND refusals, so it overstates hallucination alone. It is the closest verified proxy for regulatory-document question answering; excluded from the average.

No verified public hallucination-rate figure specific to regulatory or compliance question answering was gathered in this refresh. FinanceBench is the nearest verified proxy. Do not display a regulatory number until a source is added here.
